result.summary: The Theban chorus prays to the gods to end the plague. Oedipus proclaims a curse on Laius' unknown murderer and, after Tiresias refuses to speak, accuses him of plotting with Creon. Provoked, Tiresias names Oedipus as the killer and foretells his blindness, exile and incest.

scenes.title: The Chorus Prays for Deliverance
scenes.summary: The Theban elders pray to Apollo, Athena, Artemis, Zeus and Bacchus to end the pestilence and drive away Ares, the slayer.
scenes.stakes: The city is dying of plague; children, mothers and crops are perishing.

scenes.title: Oedipus Curses the Murderer
scenes.summary: Oedipus proclaims that anyone who knows who killed Laius must speak, and curses the killer and anyone who shields him. The Leader replies that he knows nothing and leaves the matter to Apollo.
scenes.stakes: Thebes will go on suffering unless Laius' murderer is found; those who conceal him face the curse.

scenes.title: Tiresias Is Summoned
scenes.summary: The Leader suggests consulting Tiresias. Oedipus says he has already sent for him at Creon's urging, and the blind prophet is led in.
scenes.stakes: Without a clue to the killer the plague will continue.

scenes.title: Tiresias Refuses to Speak
scenes.summary: Oedipus begs Tiresias to reveal what he knows. Tiresias laments his knowledge and refuses, until the enraged Oedipus accuses him of planning the murder.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus risks his city's salvation, and Tiresias fears speaking a terrible truth.

scenes.title: Tiresias Accuses the King
scenes.summary: Tiresias declares Oedipus himself the murderer, living in shame with his own kin. Oedipus suspects a plot by Creon and taunts the seer over the Sphinx; Tiresias predicts his fall.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus stands to lose his throne, his sight and his honour.

scenes.title: Riddling Prophecy of Ruin
scenes.summary: Oedipus orders Tiresias out. The seer hints at Oedipus' unknown parentage and foretells that the murderer will be revealed as a Theban, blind, a beggar, brother and father to his children.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus faces exposure of his birth and a downfall into blindness and exile.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas is an epithet of Athena.
Phoebus, 'bright', is a title of Apollo.
Bacchus is the Roman and Greek cult name of Dionysus.
Jove is the Roman name of Zeus.
Oedipus' phrase for the riddling Sphinx.

notable_quotes.reason: Tiresias' lament that knowledge can be a burden sets the play's central tension.
Tiresias' prophecy spells out Oedipus' incest and downfall.
Irony: the seeing king cannot see his own deeds.

analysis.text: The scene sets sight against blindness: the blind seer sees the truth while the king, proud of his eyes and wit, cannot see himself.
Greek audiences saw plague as divine pollution, and a curse or oracle carried real religious force; the chorus's prayers reflect this civic piety.

legacy.text: The blind prophet who sees truth became a lasting literary figure, echoed in T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922), which features Tiresias.

fun_facts.text: This version is Gilbert Murray's 1911 verse translation of Sophocles' play, which renders the Greek chorus in rhymed lyric.

language_notes.text: "I-e" is a Greek ritual cry (ie) used in hymns and paeans to Apollo, a call for help or praise.
The "Voice" and "Word of the Houses of Gold" is the oracle from Apollo's golden temple at Delphi, whose answer Creon has gone to fetch.
Pallas is a title of Athena. "Zeus-Child" refers to her birth from the head of Zeus; her sister here is Artemis, though Apollo's twin.
"Far-smiter" translates an epithet of Apollo, the archer god whose arrows bring plague as well as healing.
"The rocks of the dying Sun" means the west, where the sun sets; the dead are pictured flying there like flames.
Thrace, a wild northern land, was thought of as the home of Ares, god of war. The chorus wants plague driven there.
"Wolf-god" renders Lykeios, an epithet of Apollo linked with wolves.
Bacchus (Dionysus) was born at Thebes to a Theban princess. Maenads were his frenzied female followers.
"Cast my net so wide and far" means searching so widely; "clueless" here means without any clue, so he would not need to proclaim so broadly.
"Guerdon" is an archaic word for a reward.
"Shrift" is confession and absolution given by a priest; "diadem" is a royal crown.
Oedipus lists Laius's ancestors back to Cadmus, legendary founder of Thebes, to stress his duty as heir to the throne and marriage.
"Phoebus" is a title of Apollo, meaning "bright"; "God wot" means God knows.
"If of his grace he would reveal it": if the god willingly chose to reveal the murderer. Oedipus means the god cannot be forced.
"Methinks" means "it seems to me"; "'twould" is "it would." Archaic forms.
Phoebus is Apollo, god of prophecy. The Leader says Tiresias's inner sight is nearly equal to the god's.
Inverted archaic word order: "I have sent two heralds already." The two messengers show Oedipus's urgency.
"Old signs and far" means faint, distant clues from long ago that offer little help.
"The tale used to be" means this was the old report: that Laius was killed by several travellers, not one man.
"Stay close" means remain in hiding. The Leader thinks the witness will flee once he hears Oedipus's curses.
"Divineth well" means perceives or foretells truly; "divine" here is a verb meaning to discern by prophetic insight.
"Dearth of outward eyes" means lack of physical eyes: Tiresias is blind, yet sees the city's troubles inwardly.
Phoebus is Apollo; his oracle at Delphi declared the plague would end only when Laius's killer was found and punished or exiled.
"Every cry of birds" refers to augury, reading omens from birds' calls and flight, one of Tiresias's methods of prophecy.
"Compassed" means achieved; "chance or power" means whatever fortune or ability a man has.
"To veil thy mind" means to hide your thoughts or knowledge; Oedipus calls the silence unlawful and unkind.
"Lest I also stray" means lest I too go wrong, as Tiresias says Oedipus's mind does; the line trails off unfinished.
"Let thy city bleed" means let Thebes suffer the plague and ruin; bleeding stands for the city's wounds and deaths.
Even a stone's anger would be roused by Tiresias; "wrath of any stone" means the most unfeeling thing would be provoked.
"I warrant" means I assure you or I declare confidently.
"Stint" means hold back or limit; Oedipus will not restrain what he sees plainly.
"Save the blow" means except for striking it yourself; Oedipus says Tiresias planned the murder and did all but deliver the blow.
Tiresias turns Oedipus's own proclamation (the curse on the murderer's shelterers) against him: by it Oedipus must be shunned and never be spoken to.
'Thou front of brass' means 'you brazen-faced man'; 'front' is an old word for forehead or face, so brass suggests shamelessness.
'Bate' means to restrain or reduce; Oedipus asks whether Tiresias thinks he can abuse him and escape punishment.
Oedipus swears the accusation did not come from Tiresias's prophetic skill, implying someone else put him up to it.
'Twice to have stabbed at me' refers to Tiresias repeating his charge; 'stabbed' is figurative for wounding words.
"Spawn of Night" is an insult: Oedipus calls Tiresias a creature of darkness, mocking his blindness. "Free and seeing" contrasts with the blind seer.
The "She-Wolf of the woven song" is the Sphinx, who killed Thebans who failed her riddle. Oedipus solved it and freed the city.
"Sign / Where Creon bids me" means Tiresias does not put his name to or endorse whatever Creon orders; he is no one's servant but Apollo's.
The curse of a mother and father, "shod with fire," alludes to Oedipus's hidden parentage: Laius and Jocasta, whose child he killed or married.
The "bridal song" refers to Oedipus's marriage to Jocasta, his mother. Kithairon is the mountain where he was exposed as an infant.
"To brook" means to tolerate; Oedipus asks whether he must endure such words from this creature, with the sentence left grammatically incomplete in his anger.
Oedipus breaks off mid-threat, "before ...", and the Leader restrains him; the unspoken threat shows his rage.
A riddle: "give thee birth" means this day will reveal his true origin, and "blot thee out" means it will destroy him.
Refers to Oedipus solving the Sphinx's riddle, which made him king. Tiresias mocks his skill with riddles, which cannot help him now.
Laius was the former king of Thebes, whose unsolved murder is the plague's cause and what Oedipus is investigating.
"The seed, the sower and the sown" calls him child, father and husband in the same field: he sowed the same womb that bore him.

context_notes.text: The Chorus of Theban elders speaks and sings for the city, commenting on events throughout the play.
Athena protected cities, Artemis was goddess of the hunt and the moon, and Apollo was god of prophecy, healing and plague.
Ares is war personified here: the plague kills like war, yet bears no weapons.
Delphi was Apollo's oracle; its priestess's answers were treated as divine commands. Creon has brought back its reply that Laius's killer must be found.
Oedipus married Laius's widow, Jocasta, not knowing she is his mother. He claims he is acting as if for his own father.
Tiresias is the blind prophet of Thebes, famed for seeing the truth through divine insight.
Creon is Oedipus's brother-in-law, who brought the Delphic oracle's answer and advised consulting Tiresias.
The sole surviving witness of Laius's murder is a servant who escaped; he becomes crucial later.
Tiresias is the blind prophet of Thebes, famed for his seer's knowledge, and is summoned because Apollo's oracle demands the killer of Laius be found.
Laius was the former king of Thebes, whose murder went unavenged. Oedipus, unknowingly his son, now rules and seeks the killer.
Thebes is suffering a plague. Oedipus has sworn to find Laius's murderer, and the seer Tiresias is thought to know the truth.
Tiresias is blind, so "melting in thine eyes" is bitterly ironic: Oedipus appeals for pity from a man who cannot see him.
Tiresias is the blind prophet of Thebes. Oedipus summoned him to learn who killed King Laius, whose murder brought the plague.
The 'shame' hints at Oedipus's unknowing marriage to his mother Jocasta and the children born of it.
Thebes offered Oedipus the crown after he defeated the Sphinx. He fears Creon, his brother-in-law, wants it for himself.
Apollo was the god of prophecy, whose oracle at Delphi ordered Thebes to find Laius's killer. Tiresias serves him, not the king.
Tiresias is a blind prophet of Thebes, led by a boy. His sight into the truth contrasts with Oedipus' ignorance.
Oedipus believes he is a stranger from Corinth who came to Thebes. Tiresias says he is Theban-born.

literary_notes.text: The chorus addresses the unseen oracle as a living Voice, opening the ode with urgent, awed questioning.
"Dread benediction" and "Hope's daughter and Fear's" show the oracle as both blessing and terror.
Souls are "flame" and fly like birds, conveying how quickly the dead vanish.
The altars stand like a rock in a storm-tossed sea, picturing steadfast faith amid grieving waves of suffering.
Plague becomes Ares, a shrieking, fire-wrapped god standing over the speaker, making the disease a vivid hostile presence.
Oedipus unknowingly curses himself to a life of misery and exile, since he is the murderer.
Oedipus speaks of Laius as if he were his father; the audience knows he truly is, and that Oedipus is the killer.
Chance "stamped its heel" on Laius's head, picturing fate as a crushing foot.
Oedipus asks how a man can force a god. It is pious, yet ironic given how fiercely he forces the truth later.
Oedipus scorns the idea that the killer would fear words. Unknowingly, he is that killer, so his boast is dramatically ironic.
Tiresias is praised as the one in whom truth is born, setting up the contrast between his blind sight and Oedipus's seeing blindness.
"Clouds" over the city stand for the plague and trouble darkening Thebes.
Knowledge is called fearful because it brings pain without remedy, reversing the usual idea that knowing is good.
Tiresias's "mine ... and thine" hints that the evil is Oedipus's own, though Oedipus and the audience's grasp of it differs.
Claiming even a stone would be enraged exaggerates Oedipus's fury and Tiresias's supposed stubbornness.
Tiresias says Oedipus has not seen or guessed the truth; the audience knows Oedipus himself is the murderer.
Oedipus accuses the blind seer of the crime, saying only blindness prevents him from swearing it. He is the real murderer and later blinds himself.
Audiences familiar with the myth know Tiresias speaks the truth, while Oedipus still does not understand it.
Seeing 'not thyself nor them' continues the play's contrast between physical sight and true understanding.
Oedipus mocks the blind man's blindness, though he is the one spiritually blind to the truth.
Oedipus's rising paranoia and angry accusations of bribery show his pride and quick temper.
The seer is blind yet sees the truth, while the sighted king cannot see his own deeds. This reversal of sight and blindness runs through the play.
Tiresias predicts Oedipus's eyes, now bright, will turn dark, anticipating his self-blinding.
Birth and destruction come in one day, compressing Oedipus' whole fate into a single riddling line.
Oedipus' boast of having saved Thebes will be undone by the audience's knowledge that he is the polluter he seeks.
Tiresias, physically blind yet seeing the truth, predicts that the seeing king will become blind; sight and blindness are reversed.
